# Complex systems and emergence {#sec-complex-systems-and-emergence}

A complex system is a collection of many elements whose interactions produce behaviour that no element has on its
own. A magnet orders although each of its atomic moments points up or down at random when left alone. A city
segregates although none of its residents wants to live among its own kind only. A flock of birds turns as one body
although each bird watches only a few neighbours. The subject of this tutorial is how such collective behaviour arises
from simple interacting parts, how it can be described at a coarser level than the parts, and which of its features
are shared by systems as different as magnets, cities and flocks. Following @jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023 [Ch. 1],
the tutorial takes the systematic study of emergent phenomena as the defining task of complexity science.

This first chapter fixes the vocabulary that the rest of the tutorial uses, and it does so with definitions precise
enough to be checked on examples and with the few results that can be proved at this level. Its sources are the
introductory chapters of the benchmark textbooks: @thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018 [Ch. 1] for what a complex
system is, @jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023 [Part I] for emergence and the value of simple models,
@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017 [Ch. 1] and @downeyThinkComplexity2018 [Ch. 1] for models and the
distinction between complexity, randomness and chaos, @bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021 [Sec. 8.1] for sums of
many random parts, and @grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015 [Sec. 2.4], @satzMoreSumParts2022 [Ch. 10] and
@datserisNonlinearDynamicsConcise2022 [Sec. 12.1] for the logistic map and prediction.

The chapter has four sections. @sec-what-is-a-complex-system defines systems of interacting elements and, after
Thurner, Hanel and Klimek, complex systems as those whose interactions change with the states of their elements.
@sec-levels-and-emergence defines coarse-graining and levels of description, proves that the relative fluctuations of
a sum of independent parts vanish like $N^{-1/2}$, and on that basis defines emergent properties and order parameters.
@sec-models-and-their-purposes defines minimal models and proves the mean-field law of majority rule, the first
complete model of a symmetry-breaking transition in the tutorial. @sec-randomness-chaos-prediction proves the fixed
points and the onset of period two of the logistic map and defines the Lyapunov exponent, to show that chaos, like
randomness, is not by itself complexity. Results of statistical physics, such as Landau theory and the mean-field
theory of the Ising model, are stated in
[Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics](../../fundamentals-of-theoretical-physics/thermodynamics-statistical-mechanics/index.qmd#sec-landau-theory)
and are linked rather than restated.

Every definition and proposition is followed by ten examples and ten exercises, each exercise with a hidden solution
in two tabs: the argument, then a computation with its recorded output. The computations use scikit-complexity 0.9.0
throughout. The systems come from its catalogue (`skcomplex.systems`): `LogisticMapSystem`, `TentMapSystem`,
`IsingSystem`, `CurieWeissSystem`, `IdealGasSystem`, `GameOfLifeSystem`, `MajorityRuleSystem`,
`GalamMajoritySystem`, `SchellingSystem`, `CoevolvingVoterSystem`, `VicsekSystem`, `KuramotoSystem` and
`BernoulliProcessSystem`, found with `all_systems`. They are run by `simulate` (`skcomplex.core.engine.runtime`) and
measured with the analyses `stability`, `lyapunov`, `emergence`, `domains`, `distribution`, `complexity`,
`signatures` and `applicable_analyses` (`skcomplex.core.analysis`) and the experiment `orbit_diagram`
(`skcomplex.core.experiments`). NumPy is used only where the package has no ready function: block-majority
coarse-graining of a lattice, sums of independent random variables, and a few closed formulas.

## What a complex system is {#sec-what-is-a-complex-system}

Complexity science has no single agreed definition of its object, and its textbooks say so. Charbonneau declines to
define complexity at all and characterises complex systems as "many (relatively) simple individual elements
interacting locally with one another" [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 1.1]. Jensen describes them by
what they produce, properties of the whole that the parts do not have [@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Ch. 1].
Thurner, Hanel and Klimek give the most explicit description: elements with states, interactions of several types
recorded as networks, and update rules for both [@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Secs. 1.2.6 and 1.5]. This
section turns the last description into two definitions. The first covers every model of the tutorial, from a single
logistic map to a flock. The second singles out the systems whose interactions themselves change with the states of
the elements, which Thurner, Hanel and Klimek call complex in the strict sense.

For more on this topic, see @thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018 [Secs. 1.2.6, 1.5 and 1.5.1],
@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023 [Ch. 1], @charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017 [Sec. 1.1] and
@downeyThinkComplexity2018 [Ch. 1].

### Systems of interacting elements

A model of a many-part system must say what the parts are, which states each part can take, who acts on whom, and how
the states change. The definition below records exactly these four ingredients and nothing else: it forgets what the
elements are made of and keeps only their states and the pattern of their interactions. Time is discrete, $t \in
\mathbb N$, for maps and automata, and continuous, $t \geq 0$, for flows; an update rule then gives the next state or
the rate of change.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-interacting-system}
#### System of interacting elements

A **system of interacting elements** consists of the following data.

1. A finite set of **elements** $1, \dots, N$. Element $i$ has a **state set** $S_i$, its state at time $t$ is
   $s_i(t) \in S_i$, and a **microstate** is the column vector $\mathbf s = (s_1, \dots, s_N)$ in $\mathcal S = S_1
   \times \dots \times S_N$.
2. A finite set $\mathcal A$ of **interaction types** and, for each $\alpha \in \mathcal A$ and each time $t$, an $N
   \times N$ matrix $\mathbf W^\alpha(t)$ of **interaction weights** $w^\alpha_{ij}(t)$. The weight $w^\alpha_{ij}(t)
   \neq 0$ means that element $j$ acts on element $i$ through interactions of type $\alpha$ at time $t$. We write
   $\mathbf W(t) = (\mathbf W^\alpha(t))_{\alpha \in \mathcal A}$.
3. An **update rule**: functions $F_i$ that give the next state $s_i(t + 1) = F_i(\mathbf s(t), \mathbf W(t))$ (for
   discrete time) or the rate $\dot s_i(t) = F_i(\mathbf s(t), \mathbf W(t))$ (for continuous time), possibly
   depending also on random variables drawn at each step. The rule respects the weights: $F_i(\mathbf s, \mathbf W)$
   does not change when $s_j$ changes, for any $j \neq i$ with $w^\alpha_{ij} = 0$ for every $\alpha$.

The **interaction graph** at time $t$ is the directed graph on $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with an edge $j \to i$ whenever
$w^\alpha_{ij}(t) \neq 0$ for some $\alpha$ and $i \neq j$. The system is **non-interacting** if its interaction graph
has no edges at any time, so that each element evolves by a rule of its own state alone.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest system of many elements is a set of coins tossed again and again. It has elements and states but no
interactions at all, so it is the reference against which interacting systems are compared throughout the chapter.

::: {#exm-interacting-coins}
#### Repeated coin tosses

Take $N$ coins, $S_i = \{0, 1\}$, and let each coin show a fresh Bernoulli($p$) outcome at every step, independent of
everything else: $s_i(t + 1) = \xi_i(t)$ with independent $\xi_i(t) \sim \operatorname{Bern}(p)$. There are no
interaction types, $\mathcal A = \emptyset$, so the interaction graph has no edges and the system is non-interacting.
The catalogue system `BernoulliProcessSystem` of scikit-complexity is this system, with the running number of
successes of each coin as a second state.
:::

Jensen opens his discussion of emergence with the ideal gas, and it is the physical version of the coin tosses. Its
elements carry continuous states, but they still do not act on one another.

::: {#exm-interacting-ideal-gas}
#### The ideal gas

The molecules of an ideal gas are the elements, with states $s_i = (\mathbf x_i, \mathbf v_i)$, a position in the box
and a velocity. Each molecule moves freely and is reflected by the walls; the walls belong to the update rule of each
molecule, not to an interaction between molecules. The interaction graph has no edges, so the ideal gas is
non-interacting [@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Sec. 1.1]. scikit-complexity provides it as `IdealGasSystem`.
:::

A system may have a single element, and then it is trivially non-interacting, however intricate its behaviour. The
logistic map, the most famous example of chaos, is such a system, and the last section of the chapter returns to it.

::: {#exm-interacting-logistic}
#### A single logistic map

With $N = 1$, $S_1 = [0, 1]$ and $s_1(t + 1) = rs_1(t)(1 - s_1(t))$ for a parameter $0 < r \leq 4$, the logistic map
is a system of one element and no interactions. Charbonneau uses it to make the point that complicated behaviour, even
chaos, needs neither many elements nor interactions [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 1.3]. In
scikit-complexity it is `LogisticMapSystem`, with the state `map.x`.
:::

The Ising model is the first genuinely interacting system of the tutorial and the prototype of every lattice model
after it. Its interaction graph is fixed in advance by a lattice.

::: {#exm-interacting-ising}
#### The Ising model on a lattice

The elements are the $N = L^2$ sites of an $L \times L$ periodic square lattice, with $S_i = \{-1, +1\}$. There is one
interaction type, with $w_{ij} = J > 0$ when $i$ and $j$ are nearest neighbours and $w_{ij} = 0$ otherwise. In the
Metropolis update at temperature $T$ a chosen spin flips with probability $\min(1, e^{-\Delta E/T})$, where $\Delta E
= 2s_i\sum_jw_{ij}s_j$ depends only on the neighbours. The interaction graph has an edge in each direction between
neighbours, four in and four out of every site [@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Sec. 3.1]. scikit-complexity
provides it as `IsingSystem`.
:::

In the Curie-Weiss model every spin interacts with every other, each with a weak weight. This all-to-all coupling is the
structure behind every mean-field description in the tutorial.

::: {#exm-interacting-curie-weiss}
#### The Curie-Weiss model

The states are again $\pm1$, but now $w_{ij} = J/N$ for all $i \neq j$. The interaction graph is the complete directed
graph, and the field acting on spin $i$ is $\sum_{j \neq i}w_{ij}s_j = J m - Js_i/N$, with $m = \frac1N\sum_js_j$ the
magnetisation. Every spin therefore feels the same field up to a correction of order $1/N$
[@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 1.4.1]. scikit-complexity runs it with Glauber dynamics as
`CurieWeissSystem`.
:::

Cellular automata are systems of interacting elements with discrete time, finite state sets and a deterministic
rule. Conway's Game of Life is the best known of them.

::: {#exm-interacting-life}
#### Conway's Game of Life

The elements are the cells of an $L \times L$ periodic grid, $S_i = \{0, 1\}$ (dead or alive), and $w_{ij} = 1$ when
$j$ is one of the eight neighbours of $i$. With $n_i = \sum_jw_{ij}s_j$ the number of live neighbours, all cells update
at once: $s_i(t + 1) = 1$ if $s_i(t) = 1$ and $n_i \in \{2, 3\}$, or if $s_i(t) = 0$ and $n_i = 3$, and $s_i(t + 1) = 0$
otherwise. scikit-complexity provides it as `GameOfLifeSystem`, with the birth and survival counts as parameters
[@downeyThinkComplexity2018, Ch. 6].
:::

The same lattice and neighbourhood can carry a model of opinions instead of life and death. Only the rule changes, and
the definition does not distinguish physics from sociology.

::: {#exm-interacting-majority-lattice}
#### Majority rule on a lattice

In `MajorityRuleSystem` the elements are voters on a periodic grid with opinions $s_i \in \{0, 1\}$, the weights are
those of the Game of Life, and every step every voter takes the opinion held by the majority of its eight neighbours,
keeping its own opinion on a tie. The interaction graph is the same as in @exm-interacting-life; only $F_i$ differs.
:::

In Schelling's model of segregation the residents of a city move, and the interaction graph is not the one a picture of
the grid suggests. Writing the model in the form of the definition makes this visible.

::: {#exm-interacting-schelling}
#### Schelling's model of segregation

Let the elements be the cells of a grid, each empty or occupied by a resident of kind 0 or 1, so $S_i = \{\varnothing,
0, 1\}$. A resident is content if at least a threshold share of its occupied neighbours are of its kind; every step,
each discontented resident moves to an empty cell chosen at random [@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Sec. 1.1;
@downeyThinkComplexity2018, Ch. 1]. The next state of a cell depends on its neighbours (is its resident content?) but
also on every other cell (will a resident from far away move in?), so the interaction graph of this formulation is
complete. scikit-complexity provides it as `SchellingSystem`.
:::

In the Vicsek model of flocking the weights are not fixed in advance: a particle interacts with whoever is near it now.
The interaction graph therefore changes in time, as a function of the positions.

::: {#exm-interacting-vicsek}
#### The Vicsek model

Each of $N$ particles has a position $\mathbf x_i$ in a periodic box and a heading $\theta_i$. At every step it takes
the mean heading of the particles within unit distance, itself included, plus a random angle, and moves a fixed
distance along it. Here $w_{ij}(t) = 1$ if $\lVert\mathbf x_i(t) - \mathbf x_j(t)\rVert \leq 1$ and $0$ otherwise, so
the weights are a function of the states [@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Sec. 11.1]. scikit-complexity provides
it as `VicsekSystem`.
:::

The last example has several interaction types at once, as Thurner, Hanel and Klimek's banks do. Each type is a layer
of a multilayer network on the same elements.

::: {#exm-interacting-banks}
#### A network of banks

Thurner, Hanel and Klimek describe banks as elements with states such as wealth, linked by three types of interaction:
credit, derivative contracts and ownership of shares [@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 1.5, Fig. 1.4].
Here $\mathcal A = \{\text{credit}, \text{derivatives}, \text{shares}\}$, and $w^{\text{credit}}_{ij}(t)$ could be the
amount bank $j$ has lent to bank $i$. The interaction graph merges the three layers; the layers themselves form a
multilayer network.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise measures the size of the state space, which is what makes a description at the level of
microstates impractical. It compares three of the examples.

::: {#exr-interacting-count-microstates}
#### Counting microstates

Count $|\mathcal S|$ for a $10 \times 10$ Ising lattice, for a $20 \times 20$ Schelling grid with three cell states,
and for $N$ coins observed for $T$ steps (the number of possible histories). Give the decimal logarithms.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A microstate assigns one state to each element, so $|\mathcal S| = \prod_i|S_i|$. For the Ising lattice this is
$2^{100}$, with $\log_{10}2^{100} = 100\log_{10}2 \approx 30.10$. For the Schelling grid it is $3^{400}$, with
$\log_{10} = 400\log_{10}3 \approx 190.85$. A history of $N$ coins over $T$ steps is a microstate of $NT$ binary
elements, so there are $2^{NT}$ histories; for $N = 20$ and $T = 100$ this is $10^{602.06}$.

## Python

The counts are exact integers in Python, so their number of digits can be read off.

```{.python .run}
from math import log10
for name, count in [("Ising 10x10", 2**100), ("Schelling 20x20", 3**400), ("20 coins, 100 steps", 2**2000)]:
    print(f"{name}: {len(str(count))} digits, log10 = {log10(count):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
Ising 10x10: 31 digits, log10 = 30.10
Schelling 20x20: 191 digits, log10 = 190.85
20 coins, 100 steps: 603 digits, log10 = 602.06
```
::::
:::

The interaction graph is read off the weights. The second exercise counts its edges for the two lattices of the
examples and checks the count by building the weight matrix.

::: {#exr-interacting-lattice-graph}
#### Edges of lattice interaction graphs

Show that the interaction graph of the Ising model on an $L \times L$ periodic lattice ($L \geq 3$) has $4L^2$ directed
edges and that of the Game of Life has $8L^2$. Check both counts for $L = 5$ from the weight matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $L \geq 3$ the four nearest neighbours of a site on the torus are distinct sites, and the eight Moore neighbours
are distinct as well. Each site therefore receives an edge from exactly four sites in the Ising model and from exactly
eight in the Game of Life. Summing the in-degrees over the $L^2$ sites gives $4L^2$ and $8L^2$ directed edges.

## Python

Check on $L = 5$: the weight matrices are built from the shifts of the torus and their non-zero entries counted.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
L = 5
idx = np.arange(L * L).reshape(L, L)
def weights(shifts):
    W = np.zeros((L * L, L * L), dtype=int)
    for dx, dy in shifts:
        W[idx.ravel(), np.roll(idx, (dx, dy), axis=(0, 1)).ravel()] = 1
    return W
von_neumann = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]
moore = [(a, b) for a in (-1, 0, 1) for b in (-1, 0, 1) if (a, b) != (0, 0)]
print("Ising edges:", weights(von_neumann).sum(), "= 4L^2 =", 4 * L * L)
print("Life edges:", weights(moore).sum(), "= 8L^2 =", 8 * L * L)
```

```{.text .run-output}
Ising edges: 100 = 4L^2 = 100
Life edges: 200 = 8L^2 = 200
```
::::
:::

A non-interacting system is the sum of its parts in the most literal sense: its elements are statistically
independent. The third exercise proves this for stochastic rules and checks it on the coin tosses.

::: {#exr-interacting-independence}
#### Independence of non-interacting elements

Let a non-interacting system in discrete time have update rules $s_i(t + 1) = F_i(s_i(t), \xi_i(t))$, where the random
inputs $\xi_i(t)$ are independent for all $i$ and $t$ and independent of the initial states, and let the initial states
$s_1(0), \dots, s_N(0)$ be independent. Prove that the trajectories $(s_i(t))_{t \geq 0}$ of different elements are
independent.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By induction on $t$, $s_i(t)$ is a function of $s_i(0), \xi_i(0), \dots, \xi_i(t - 1)$ only, because $F_i$ reads no
other element. So the whole trajectory of element $i$ up to time $T$ is a function $g_i$ of the family $Z_i = (s_i(0),
\xi_i(0), \dots, \xi_i(T - 1))$. The families $Z_1, \dots, Z_N$ are independent, since they are made of disjoint sets of
independent variables, and functions of independent families are independent. Hence the trajectories up to any $T$
are independent, which is the claim.

## Python

Check on `BernoulliProcessSystem`: for 2000 coins tossed 100 times with $p = 0.3$, the success counts of coins $2k$
and $2k + 1$ should be uncorrelated, while each count has mean $30$ and variance $21$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.stochastic_processes import BernoulliProcessSystem
run = simulate(BernoulliProcessSystem(2000, p=0.3), until=100, random_state=1)
counts = run.get_agents("trials", 100).values["successes"]
print(f"mean {counts.mean():.2f}, variance {counts.var():.2f}")
print(f"correlation of neighbouring coins: {np.corrcoef(counts[0::2], counts[1::2])[0, 1]:+.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean 30.04, variance 19.92
correlation of neighbouring coins: -0.032
```
::::
:::

The Metropolis rule of the Ising model must respect the weights, as the definition requires. The fourth exercise shows
that the energy change of a flip depends on the neighbours only.

::: {#exr-interacting-ising-flip}
#### The energy change of a spin flip

The Ising energy is $E(\mathbf s) = -\sum_{i < j}w_{ij}s_is_j - h\sum_is_i$ with symmetric weights. Prove that flipping
spin $i$ changes the energy by $\Delta E = 2s_i(\sum_jw_{ij}s_j + h)$, so the Metropolis rule for spin $i$ reads only
the states of the elements that act on $i$. Check the formula on a random $8 \times 8$ configuration.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The terms of $E$ that contain $s_i$ are $-s_i\sum_{j \neq i}w_{ij}s_j - hs_i$, using $w_{ij} = w_{ji}$. Flipping $s_i
\to -s_i$ changes only these terms, and changes their sign, so $\Delta E = E(\text{after}) - E(\text{before}) =
2s_i\sum_jw_{ij}s_j + 2hs_i$, with $s_i$ the value before the flip. Only the $s_j$ with $w_{ij} \neq 0$ enter.

## Python

Check on a random configuration of an $8 \times 8$ torus with $J = 1$ and $h = 0.3$: the energy difference is computed
directly for every site and compared with the formula.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
L, J, h = 8, 1.0, 0.3
s = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=(L, L))
def energy(s):
    bonds = s * np.roll(s, 1, 0) + s * np.roll(s, 1, 1)
    return -J * bonds.sum() - h * s.sum()
neighbours = sum(np.roll(s, k, a) for k in (1, -1) for a in (0, 1))
worst = 0.0
for i in range(L):
    for j in range(L):
        t = s.copy(); t[i, j] *= -1
        worst = max(worst, abs((energy(t) - energy(s)) - 2 * s[i, j] * (J * neighbours[i, j] + h)))
print("largest discrepancy over 64 sites:", worst)
```

```{.text .run-output}
largest discrepancy over 64 sites: 1.7763568394002505e-15
```
::::
:::

A cellular automaton is a deterministic system of interacting elements, and its behaviour can be followed exactly by
hand. The fifth exercise does so for the smallest oscillator of the Game of Life.

::: {#exr-interacting-blinker}
#### The blinker

On a $5 \times 5$ torus, start the Game of Life from three live cells in a horizontal row in the middle. Compute the
next two states by hand, and check them with `GameOfLifeSystem`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Let the live cells be $(2, 1), (2, 2), (2, 3)$ (row, column). The centre has two live neighbours and survives; the two
end cells have one live neighbour each and die. The cells $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 2)$ above and below the centre have three
live neighbours and are born, and no other dead cell has three. So the next state is the vertical row $(1, 2), (2, 2),
(3, 2)$. By the same count rotated by a quarter turn, the state after that is the horizontal row again: the blinker
has period 2.

## Python

The initial cells are passed to `GameOfLifeSystem`, and the lattice of each frame is printed.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.computer_science.automata import GameOfLifeSystem
start = np.zeros((5, 5)); start[2, 1:4] = 1
frames = simulate(GameOfLifeSystem((5, 5), initial=start), until=2).get_lattice("cells.alive")
for t in range(3):
    print(f"t = {t}:", ["".join("#" if c else "." for c in row) for row in frames[t].astype(int)])
print("period 2:", bool((frames[2] == frames[0]).all()) and not bool((frames[1] == frames[0]).all()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
t = 0: ['.....', '.....', '.###.', '.....', '.....']
t = 1: ['.....', '..#..', '..#..', '..#..', '.....']
t = 2: ['.....', '.....', '.###.', '.....', '.....']
period 2: True
```
::::
:::

The Curie-Weiss weights make every spin see almost the same field. The sixth exercise proves the formula for the field
and checks how small the individual correction is.

::: {#exr-interacting-curie-weiss-field}
#### The field in the Curie-Weiss model

With $w_{ij} = J/N$ for $i \neq j$, prove that the field $h_i = \sum_{j \neq i}w_{ij}s_j$ on spin $i$ equals $Jm -
Js_i/N$, and conclude that $\max_i|h_i - Jm| = J/N$. Check this on a random configuration of 500 spins drawn by
`CurieWeissSystem`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$h_i = \frac JN\sum_{j \neq i}s_j = \frac JN(\sum_js_j - s_i) = Jm - \frac JNs_i$. Since $|s_i| = 1$, every $|h_i - Jm|$
equals $J/N$. The rule of spin $i$ thus depends on the other spins only through the single number $m$, up to a
correction that vanishes as $N \to \infty$; this is why mean-field theory is exact for this model, as
[Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics](../../fundamentals-of-theoretical-physics/thermodynamics-statistical-mechanics/index.qmd#prp-curie-weiss-exact)
proves.

## Python

Check on the initial configuration of `CurieWeissSystem(500)` with $J = 1$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import CurieWeissSystem
N, J = 500, 1.0
s = simulate(CurieWeissSystem(N, J=J), until=1, random_state=3).get_values("spins.spin")[0]
m = s.mean()
h = (J / N) * (s.sum() - s)
print(f"m = {m:+.3f}; max |h_i - J m| = {np.abs(h - J * m).max():.4f}; J/N = {J / N:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
m = +0.100; max |h_i - J m| = 0.0020; J/N = 0.0020
```
::::
:::

A majority rule with ties kept has configurations that never change and configurations that oscillate. The seventh
exercise finds one of each on the lattice of @exm-interacting-majority-lattice.

::: {#exr-interacting-majority-patterns}
#### Fixed and oscillating patterns of majority rule

For the majority rule on an $L \times L$ torus with $L$ even and eight neighbours, show that the checkerboard is fixed
and that horizontal stripes of width one have period 2. Check both with `MajorityRuleSystem` for $L = 6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

In a checkerboard the four diagonal neighbours of a cell have its opinion and the four orthogonal ones the other
opinion: a tie, so every voter keeps its opinion and the configuration is fixed. In horizontal stripes a cell agrees
with its two horizontal neighbours and disagrees with the three cells above and the three below: six against two, so
every voter switches. The switched configuration is the complementary stripe pattern, which switches back at the next
step, so the period is 2 (it is not 1 because every cell changes).

## Python

The two patterns are passed as initial opinions through the `initial_state` argument of `simulate`.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.social.opinion_dynamics import MajorityRuleSystem
L = 6
checker = (np.indices((L, L)).sum(0) % 2).astype(bool)
stripes = np.zeros((L, L), dtype=bool); stripes[::2] = True
for name, start in [("checkerboard", checker), ("stripes", stripes)]:
    run = simulate(MajorityRuleSystem((L, L)), until=2, initial_state={"voters.opinion": start.ravel()})
    f = run.get_lattice("voters.opinion")
    print(f"{name}: unchanged after 1 step {bool((f[1] == f[0]).all())}, after 2 steps {bool((f[2] == f[0]).all())}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
checkerboard: unchanged after 1 step True, after 2 steps True
stripes: unchanged after 1 step False, after 2 steps True
```
::::
:::

The interaction graph of the Vicsek model is a function of the positions, so it changes as the particles move. The
eighth exercise measures that change.

::: {#exr-interacting-vicsek-graph}
#### The changing graph of a flock

Run `VicsekSystem` with 300 particles in a box of side 10 at noise $\eta = 0.1$ for 100 steps. Compute the number of
pairs within unit distance (on the torus) at the first and last frames, and the fraction of the first frame's pairs
that are still pairs at the end.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Two particles interact at time $t$ when the periodic distance between them is at most 1. With the positions of a
frame, the distance on the torus of side $\ell$ is computed from the coordinate differences $d \mapsto d - \ell
\operatorname{round}(d/\ell)$. Counting pairs at two frames and intersecting the two sets of pairs measures how much
the interaction graph has changed. In a flock that forms, neighbours change while the particles align, so the two sets
of pairs share only part of their members.

## Python

The positions are read from the state `flock.x` of the run.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.active_matter import VicsekSystem
side = 10.0
run = simulate(VicsekSystem(300, size=side, eta=0.1, seed=4), until=100, random_state=4)
x = run.get_values("flock.x")
def pairs(pos):
    d = pos[:, None, :] - pos[None, :, :]
    d -= side * np.round(d / side)
    close = (d ** 2).sum(-1) <= 1.0
    return {(i, j) for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(np.triu(close, 1)))}
first, last = pairs(x[0]), pairs(x[-1])
print(f"pairs at t = 0: {len(first)}, at t = 100: {len(last)}, kept: {len(first & last) / len(first):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
pairs at t = 0: 1413, at t = 100: 9309, kept: 0.29
```
::::
:::

Two logistic maps can be coupled so that each feels the other. The ninth exercise writes the coupled pair as a system
of interacting elements and shows that the coupling can synchronise two chaotic elements.

::: {#exr-interacting-coupled-maps}
#### Two coupled logistic maps

Let $f(x) = 4x(1 - x)$ and $x' = (1 - \varepsilon)f(x) + \varepsilon f(y)$, $y' = (1 - \varepsilon)f(y) + \varepsilon
f(x)$. Give the interaction weights, and show that the difference $u = x - y$ obeys $u' = (1 - 2\varepsilon)(f(x) -
f(y))$. Compute $|x - y|$ after 2000 steps for $\varepsilon = 0$ and $\varepsilon = 0.4$, from $x = 0.3$, $y = 0.31$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With one interaction type, $w_{12} = w_{21} = \varepsilon$: each map acts on the other with weight $\varepsilon$, and
for $\varepsilon = 0$ the system is non-interacting. Subtracting the two rules, $x' - y' = (1 - \varepsilon)(f(x) -
f(y)) - \varepsilon(f(x) - f(y)) = (1 - 2\varepsilon)(f(x) - f(y))$. Near the diagonal $f(x) - f(y) \approx
f'(x)u$, so a small difference is multiplied at each step by $(1 - 2\varepsilon)f'(x)$. For $\varepsilon = 0.4$ the
factor $1 - 2\varepsilon = 0.2$ outweighs the average stretching of $f$ (a factor $2$ per step on average, as the
last section of the chapter shows), so the two maps synchronise; for $\varepsilon = 0$ they stay apart.

## Python

The pair is iterated with NumPy, since only the rule is needed.

```{.python .run}
f = lambda x: 4 * x * (1 - x)
for eps in (0.0, 0.4):
    x, y = 0.3, 0.31
    for _ in range(2000):
        x, y = (1 - eps) * f(x) + eps * f(y), (1 - eps) * f(y) + eps * f(x)
    print(f"eps = {eps}: |x - y| = {abs(x - y):.3e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
eps = 0.0: |x - y| = 1.047e-01
eps = 0.4: |x - y| = 0.000e+00
```
::::
:::

The definition requires each update rule to respect the weights. The tenth exercise proves the consequence that makes
the non-interacting version of any system well defined, which the next section relies on.

::: {#exr-interacting-switch-off}
#### Switching the interactions off

Let $F_i$ be the update rule of a system of interacting elements. Prove that $F_i(\mathbf s, \mathbf 0)$, the rule with
all weights set to zero, depends on $\mathbf s$ only through $s_i$, so that "the same elements with the interactions
removed" is a non-interacting system. Check this for the Game of Life: with no neighbours the rule kills every cell.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

With $\mathbf W = \mathbf 0$, every $w^\alpha_{ij}$ with $j \neq i$ is zero. By item 3 of @def-interacting-system,
$F_i(\mathbf s, \mathbf 0)$ does not change when $s_j$ changes, for every $j \neq i$. Changing the coordinates of
$\mathbf s$ other than $s_i$ one at a time therefore leaves $F_i(\mathbf s, \mathbf 0)$ unchanged, so it is a function
of $s_i$ alone. For the Game of Life, $n_i = 0$ for all cells when the weights vanish, and the rule gives $s_i(t + 1) =
0$ in both cases ($0 \notin \{2, 3\}$ and $0 \neq 3$).

## Python

Check on a random $20 \times 20$ grid: the non-interacting rule is the life-like rule with no birth counts and no
survival counts, which `GameOfLifeSystem` accepts as parameters.

```{.python .run}
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.computer_science.automata import GameOfLifeSystem
frames = simulate(GameOfLifeSystem((20, 20), born=(), survive=(), random_state=5), until=2).get_lattice("cells.alive")
print("live cells:", [int(f.sum()) for f in frames])
```

```{.text .run-output}
live cells: [127, 0, 0]
```
::::
:::
::::

### Complex systems

In most of the examples above the weights are fixed in advance: the lattice of the Ising model and of the Game of
Life never changes. In the Vicsek model, Schelling's city and the network of banks, the states decide who interacts
with whom, and the interactions decide how the states change. Thurner, Hanel and Klimek make this mutual dependence,
which they call co-evolution, the defining feature of complex systems: "the state of the network determines the
future states of the nodes" and "the state of the nodes determines the future state of the links"
[@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 1.5.1]. The definition below adds to @def-interacting-system an update
rule for the weights that reads the states.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-complex-system}
#### Complex system

A **complex system**, in the sense of Thurner, Hanel and Klimek, is a system of interacting elements
(@def-interacting-system) whose interaction weights also evolve by a rule that depends on the states: there are
functions $\mathbf G^\alpha$ with
$$
\mathbf W^\alpha(t + 1) = \mathbf G^\alpha(\mathbf s(t), \mathbf W(t)) \quad\text{or}\quad \dot{\mathbf W}^\alpha(t)
= \mathbf G^\alpha(\mathbf s(t), \mathbf W(t)),
$$
possibly random, and for some $\alpha$ and some $\mathbf W$ the value $\mathbf G^\alpha(\mathbf s, \mathbf W)$ is not
the same for all microstates $\mathbf s$. States and interactions then **co-evolve**: the weights determine how the
states change, and the states determine how the weights change.
:::

::::

The definition is narrower than common usage. Jensen calls complex any system of interacting components whose
aggregate has properties the components lack, and the Ising model is his first example
[@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Secs. 1.2 and 3.1]. In that wider sense every interacting system of this tutorial
is a complex system, and the chapters use the word so. The definition above isolates what Thurner, Hanel and Klimek
consider the hard core of the subject: systems "described with the first equation alone are not called complex,
however complicated they may be" [@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 1.5.1].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example applies the definition to the Ising model, the system of @exm-interacting-ising. Its weights are
constant, so the definition gives a clear negative answer.

::: {#exm-complex-ising-not}
#### The Ising model is not complex in this sense

The weights of the Ising model are fixed by the lattice: $\mathbf W(t + 1) = \mathbf W(t)$. The rule $\mathbf G(\mathbf
s, \mathbf W) = \mathbf W$ does not depend on $\mathbf s$, so the Ising model is a system of interacting elements but
not a complex system in the sense of @def-complex-system, however rich its phase transition. The same holds for the
Game of Life and for majority rule on a lattice.
:::

The Vicsek model is complex in the strict sense, because its weights are computed from the positions. This shows that
co-evolution can be built into the geometry of a model without a separate rule for the links.

::: {#exm-complex-vicsek}
#### Flocks co-evolve with their neighbourhoods

In the Vicsek model of @exm-interacting-vicsek, $w_{ij}(t + 1) = 1$ if $\lVert\mathbf x_i(t + 1) - \mathbf x_j(t +
1)\rVert \leq 1$, where the new positions are computed from $\mathbf s(t)$. So $\mathbf W(t + 1) = \mathbf
G(\mathbf s(t))$, with $\mathbf G$ depending on the positions and headings. Headings change through the weights, and
weights through the headings: the model is a complex system.
:::

Schelling's model is complex for the same reason. Its weights, the neighbourhoods of the residents, change every time a
resident moves.

::: {#exm-complex-schelling}
#### Segregation co-evolves with neighbourhoods

Writing Schelling's model with the residents as elements (rather than the cells), a resident's state is its kind and
its location, and $w_{ij} = 1$ when residents $i$ and $j$ live in neighbouring cells. A discontented resident moves,
which changes its row of weights; whether it is content depends on its neighbours' kinds through those weights. The
two equations of @def-complex-system are both present [@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 1.4.1].
:::

The co-evolving voter model is the standard minimal example of co-evolution in social dynamics. It is in the
catalogue of scikit-complexity as `CoevolvingVoterSystem`.

::: {#exm-complex-coevolving-voter}
#### The co-evolving voter model

Voters with binary opinions sit on the nodes of a random graph. At each step an active voter with a disagreeing
neighbour either copies that neighbour's opinion, with probability $1 - q$, or, with probability $q$, cuts the link and
rewires it to a voter who agrees with it. The first move changes a state through the weights, the second a weight
through the states [@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 4.8.7]. Above a critical rewiring probability the
network splits into groups of one opinion.
:::

Thurner, Hanel and Klimek illustrate the definition with banks, where wealth and contracts change each other. The same
example also has a part that is not complex.

::: {#exm-complex-banks}
#### Wealth, contracts and the gender of a chief executive

In the bank network of @exm-interacting-banks, a poor bank may not issue new credit, so the credit weights depend on
wealth; and the portfolio of contracts determines the bank's profit, so wealth depends on the weights. The wealth and
credit network form a complex system. The gender of a bank's chief executive, a second state, neither affects the
network nor is affected by it; the system of genders and links is not complex
[@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 1.5].
:::

Learning in neural networks is a form of co-evolution. Hebb's rule strengthens the connection between two neurons that
are active together.

::: {#exm-complex-hebb}
#### Hebbian learning

Let neurons have states $s_i = \pm1$ and update by $s_i(t + 1) = \operatorname{sign}(\sum_jw_{ij}s_j(t))$, and let the
weights follow Hebb's rule $w_{ij}(t + 1) = w_{ij}(t) + \eta s_i(t)s_j(t)$ for $i \neq j$, with a learning rate $\eta
> 0$. The weight rule reads the states, so the network is a complex system in the sense of the definition. Repeated
presentation of a pattern stores it in the weights.
:::

Evolutionary models make the set of interactions change because the interacting entities themselves change. Jensen's
Tangled Nature model is of this kind.

::: {#exm-complex-tangled-nature}
#### Ecosystems of evolving species

In the Tangled Nature model, individuals of many types reproduce with a probability that depends on interactions
between their type and the types present, and offspring mutate into new types
[@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Secs. 3.4 and 11.3]. The interactions that matter at a given time are those
among the types present, so the effective weight matrix changes as types appear and go extinct, and those events are
decided by the states. Jensen shows that this co-evolution produces long quiet periods broken by abrupt changes of
the whole ecosystem.
:::

When the weights change much more slowly than the states, the states see almost fixed weights. Thurner, Hanel and
Klimek note that this separation of time scales is what makes some complex systems tractable
[@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 1.5.1, footnote 4].

::: {#exm-complex-time-scales}
#### Separation of time scales

Suppose $\dot{\mathbf W} = \epsilon\mathbf G(\mathbf s, \mathbf W)$ with a small $\epsilon > 0$. Over times much
shorter than $1/\epsilon$ the weights are nearly constant, and the states evolve as in a system with fixed weights;
over longer times the weights follow the average of $\mathbf G$ over the states the fast dynamics visits. Learning in
the brain (slow synapses, fast neurons) and the formation of social ties (slow) under opinion dynamics (fast) are
examples.
:::

The weights of a complex system can be random as well as deterministic. Rewiring in the voter model is random, and so
is the meeting of agents in a market.

::: {#exm-complex-random-meetings}
#### Random encounters

Let agents with wealth $s_i$ meet in random pairs at every step and exchange a fraction of their wealth, with richer
agents more likely to be chosen as partners: $w_{ij}(t) = 1$ if $i$ and $j$ meet at time $t$, drawn with a probability
increasing in $s_i$ and $s_j$. The weights are random, with a law that depends on the states, so this is a complex
system; with partners drawn without regard to wealth, the weights would be random but independent of the states, and
the system would not be complex in the sense of @def-complex-system.
:::

The scikit-complexity catalogue records the kind of each system, and a search by topic finds the co-evolving ones. The
last example runs such a search.

::: {#exm-complex-catalogue}
#### Finding co-evolving systems in the catalogue

The catalogue function `all_systems` lists systems by field and topic. Among the systems tagged `adaptive network`
are co-evolving voter and epidemic models, whose links are rewired according to the states of their nodes.

```{.python .run}
from skcomplex.systems import all_systems
print(sorted(name for name, _ in all_systems(topics="adaptive network")))
```

```{.text .run-output}
['AdaptiveDelayNetworkSystem', 'AdaptiveFlowNetworkSystem', 'AdaptiveKuramotoSystem', 'AdaptiveSISSystem', 'CoevolvingVoterSystem', 'JainKrishnaSystem', 'JoinAClubSystem', 'STDPNetworkSystem', 'SequentiallyLinearEcosystemSystem', 'SoleManrubiaSystem', 'TwoLayerSepsisSystem']
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise applies the definition to five small systems. Each answer is a check of whether the weights have a
rule and whether that rule reads the states.

::: {#exr-complex-classify}
#### Which systems are complex?

Decide which of the following are complex systems in the sense of @def-complex-system: (a) the Curie-Weiss model; (b)
the Vicsek model; (c) an epidemic on a fixed contact network; (d) an epidemic in which susceptible people cut their
links to infected contacts; (e) Kuramoto oscillators whose coupling strengths are fixed in advance but change with time
on a prescribed schedule $w_{ij}(t) = K(t)/N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) No: the weights $J/N$ are constant. (b) Yes (@exm-complex-vicsek). (c) No: the contact network is fixed. (d) Yes:
links are removed according to the states of their ends. (e) No: the weights change, but $\mathbf G$ depends only on
$t$, not on the states. Only (b) and (d) have weights that read the states.

## Python

The catalogue's topic tag `adaptive network` gives a partial cross-check: it marks systems with an explicit rule for
rewiring links, such as the co-evolving voter model. The Vicsek model is complex without carrying the tag, because its
links follow from the positions rather than from a separate rule.

```{.python .run}
from skcomplex.systems import all_systems
adaptive = {name for name, _ in all_systems(topics="adaptive network")}
for name in ["CurieWeissSystem", "VicsekSystem", "CoevolvingVoterSystem", "KuramotoSystem"]:
    print(f"{name}: tagged adaptive network = {name in adaptive}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
CurieWeissSystem: tagged adaptive network = False
VicsekSystem: tagged adaptive network = False
CoevolvingVoterSystem: tagged adaptive network = True
KuramotoSystem: tagged adaptive network = False
```
::::
:::

When the weight rule ignores the states, the weights follow a schedule fixed by the initial weights. The second
exercise proves this and contrasts it with Hebb's rule.

::: {#exr-complex-schedule}
#### Weights that do not read the states

Prove that if $\mathbf G$ does not depend on $\mathbf s$, then $\mathbf W(t)$ is a function of $\mathbf W(0)$ and $t$
alone (for a deterministic rule in discrete time), so the system is a system of interacting elements with prescribed
time-dependent weights. Then show that Hebb's rule of @exm-complex-hebb with a fixed pattern $\mathbf s$ gives
$w_{ij}(t) = w_{ij}(0) + \eta ts_is_j$, which depends on the pattern.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $\mathbf W(t + 1) = \mathbf G(\mathbf W(t))$, then by induction $\mathbf W(t) = \mathbf G^t(\mathbf W(0))$, the
$t$-fold composition, which involves no state. Under Hebb's rule with $\mathbf s(t) = \mathbf s$ held fixed, each step
adds $\eta s_is_j$ to $w_{ij}$, so after $t$ steps $w_{ij}(t) = w_{ij}(0) + \eta ts_is_j$. Two patterns that differ in
the sign of $s_is_j$ produce different weights, so this $\mathbf G$ reads the states.

## Python

Check on a pattern of 6 neurons with $\eta = 0.1$ and 10 steps from zero weights.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
s = np.array([1, -1, 1, 1, -1, -1])
W = np.zeros((6, 6)); eta = 0.1
for _ in range(10):
    W += eta * np.outer(s, s); np.fill_diagonal(W, 0)
expected = 10 * eta * np.outer(s, s); np.fill_diagonal(expected, 0)
print("W(10) equals eta t s_i s_j:", np.allclose(W, expected))
print("row of neuron 0:", W[0].round(2))
```

```{.text .run-output}
W(10) equals eta t s_i s_j: True
row of neuron 0: [ 0. -1.  1.  1. -1. -1.]
```
::::
:::

The co-evolving voter model removes disagreement in two ways: by persuasion and by cutting links. The third exercise
measures the disagreeing links over a run of `CoevolvingVoterSystem`.

::: {#exr-complex-voter-discordant}
#### Disagreement in the co-evolving voter model

Run `CoevolvingVoterSystem` with 200 voters, mean degree 4 and rewiring probability $q = 0.6$ for 100 steps. Count the
links whose ends disagree at times 0, 25, 50 and 100, and the number of links. Explain why the number of links stays
the same.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A rewiring step removes one link and adds one, and a copying step changes an opinion and no link, so the number of
links is conserved. Rewiring turns a disagreeing link into an agreeing one; copying changes the disagreement of all
links at the copying voter. With $q = 0.6$, above the critical value near $0.38$ for mean degree 4, rewiring wins and
the disagreeing links disappear: the network splits into groups of one opinion.

## Python

The network of a frame is read with `get_network`, and the opinions with `get_values`.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.social.opinion_dynamics import CoevolvingVoterSystem
run = simulate(CoevolvingVoterSystem(200, mean_degree=4, rewiring=0.6), until=100, random_state=0)
opinion = run.get_values("voters.opinion")
for t in (0, 25, 50, 100):
    net = run.get_network(t)
    a, b = np.asarray(net.sources), np.asarray(net.targets)
    print(f"t = {t:3d}: links {len(a)}, disagreeing {int((opinion[t][a] != opinion[t][b]).sum())}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t =   0: links 388, disagreeing 183
t =  25: links 388, disagreeing 42
t =  50: links 388, disagreeing 16
t = 100: links 388, disagreeing 2
```
::::
:::

In the Vicsek model the mean number of neighbours is set by the density and by how the flock clusters. The fourth
exercise follows the mean degree of the interaction graph while a flock forms.

::: {#exr-complex-vicsek-degree}
#### Clustering raises the number of neighbours

For particles placed uniformly at random in a box of side $\ell$, the expected number of other particles within unit
distance is $(N - 1)\pi/\ell^2$. Compute it for $N = 300$ and $\ell = 10$, and compare with the mean degree of the
Vicsek interaction graph at times 0 and 200 for $\eta = 0.1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each of the other $N - 1$ particles is within unit distance with probability $\pi/\ell^2$ (the area of the unit disc
over the area of the box, ignoring the boundary, which is periodic), so the expected degree is $299\pi/100 \approx
9.39$. The initial positions are uniform, so the degree at $t = 0$ is close to this. As the flock forms, particles
gather in dense moving bands, and since the weights follow the positions, the mean degree grows: the states have
changed the interaction graph.

## Python

The degrees are computed from the positions `flock.x` with the periodic distance.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.active_matter import VicsekSystem
side, N = 10.0, 300
x = simulate(VicsekSystem(N, size=side, eta=0.1, seed=7), until=200, random_state=7).get_values("flock.x")
def mean_degree(pos):
    d = pos[:, None, :] - pos[None, :, :]
    d -= side * np.round(d / side)
    return (((d ** 2).sum(-1) <= 1.0).sum() - N) / N
print(f"uniform expectation {(N - 1) * np.pi / side**2:.2f}; t = 0: {mean_degree(x[0]):.2f}; t = 200: {mean_degree(x[-1]):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
uniform expectation 9.39; t = 0: 9.15; t = 200: 55.92
```
::::
:::

Schelling's residents change their neighbourhoods by moving, and that is what makes the model complex. The fifth
exercise counts the moves over a run and the resulting change of neighbourhoods.

::: {#exr-complex-schelling-moves}
#### Moving residents rewire the city

Run `SchellingSystem` on a $20 \times 20$ grid with density $0.8$, a minority share of $0.3$ and threshold $0.5$ for 50
steps. Using the residents' locations, count how many residents are at a different cell at the end than at the start,
and compute the mean share of like neighbours at both times.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The share of like neighbours of a resident is the number of occupied neighbouring cells (of the eight) holding its
kind, divided by the number of occupied neighbouring cells. Initially kinds are placed at random, so a majority
resident has on average about $0.7$ like neighbours and a minority resident about $0.3$, about $0.6$ over all
residents; minority residents are mostly discontented and move. Each move changes the weights of the mover and of its old and new neighbours, so many rows of
the weight matrix change, and the mean like share rises well above its initial value.

## Python

The kinds and locations of the residents at a frame come from `get_agents`.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.social.segregation import SchellingSystem
run = simulate(SchellingSystem(20, 20, density=0.8, minority=0.3, threshold=0.5), until=50, random_state=0)
def state(frame):
    agents = run.get_agents("residents", frame)
    return np.asarray(agents.ids), np.asarray(agents.values["kind"]), np.asarray(agents.locations)
def like_share(kind, loc):
    grid = -np.ones((20, 20)); grid[loc[:, 0], loc[:, 1]] = kind
    shares = []
    for k, (r, c) in zip(kind, loc):
        nb = [grid[(r + a) % 20, (c + b) % 20] for a in (-1, 0, 1) for b in (-1, 0, 1) if (a, b) != (0, 0)]
        nb = [v for v in nb if v >= 0]
        shares.append(np.mean([v == k for v in nb]) if nb else 1.0)
    return np.mean(shares)
ids0, kind0, loc0 = state(0)
ids1, kind1, loc1 = state(len(run.times) - 1)
start = dict(zip(ids0, map(tuple, loc0))); end = dict(zip(ids1, map(tuple, loc1)))
print(f"residents: {len(ids0)}, moved: {sum(start[i] != end[i] for i in ids0)}")
print(f"mean like share: start {like_share(kind0, loc0):.2f}, end {like_share(kind1, loc1):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
residents: 320, moved: 106
mean like share: start 0.64, end 0.89
```
::::
:::

A multilayer network with many elements has a very large number of weights, and that is one reason why complex systems
are studied through coarse descriptions. The sixth exercise counts them.

::: {#exr-complex-weight-count}
#### How many weights?

A system has $N$ elements and $|\mathcal A|$ interaction types, with no self-interactions. How many weights
$w^\alpha_{ij}$ does a microstate of its weights have? Evaluate for the bank network of @exm-complex-banks with $N =
5000$ banks and three types, and compare with the number of states (one wealth per bank).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

For each type there is one weight per ordered pair $i \neq j$, so $|\mathcal A|N(N - 1)$ weights. For $N = 5000$ and
three types this is $3 \cdot 5000 \cdot 4999 \approx 7.5 \times 10^7$, against $5000$ states: the weights outnumber the
states by a factor $3(N - 1) \approx 1.5 \times 10^4$. A co-evolving system must update all of them.

## Python

The counts are evaluated directly.

```{.python .run}
N, types = 5000, 3
weights = types * N * (N - 1)
print(f"weights: {weights:,}; states: {N:,}; ratio: {weights / N:,.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
weights: 74,985,000; states: 5,000; ratio: 14,997
```
::::
:::

When the weights change slowly, the states relax to what the current weights dictate. The seventh exercise proves this
for a linear toy model and checks it numerically.

::: {#exr-complex-slow-weights}
#### Slow weights, fast states

Consider $\dot s = -s + w$ and $\dot w = \epsilon(c - s)$ for constants $c$ and $0 < \epsilon < 1/4$. Show that the
fixed point is $s = w = c$ and that it is attracting, and that for small $\epsilon$ the state follows the weight,
$s(t) - w(t) \to 0$ on the fast time scale. Integrate from $s = 0$, $w = 2$ with $c = 1$, $\epsilon = 0.05$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The rates vanish when $w = s$ and $s = c$. The system is linear in $(s - c, w - c)$ with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-1 &
1\\ -\epsilon & 0\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues solve $\mu^2 + \mu + \epsilon = 0$: $\mu = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1 -
4\epsilon}}{2}$, both negative for $0 < \epsilon < 1/4$, so the fixed point attracts. The eigenvalue near $-1$ is the
fast relaxation of $s$ towards $w$; the one near $-\epsilon$ is the slow drift of $w$ towards $c$. So after a time of
order 1, $s \approx w$, and both then approach $c$ over a time of order $1/\epsilon$.

## Python

The two equations are integrated by Euler steps of $0.01$.

```{.python .run}
s, w, c, eps, dt = 0.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.05, 0.01
for step in range(1, 20001):
    s, w = s + dt * (-s + w), w + dt * eps * (c - s)
    if step in (500, 2000, 20000):
        print(f"t = {step * dt:5.0f}: s = {s:.4f}, w = {w:.4f}, s - w = {s - w:+.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t =     5: s = 1.8853, w = 1.8552, s - w = +0.0300
t =    20: s = 1.4094, w = 1.3878, s - w = +0.0216
t =   200: s = 1.0000, w = 1.0000, s - w = +0.0000
```
::::
:::

A minimal bank model shows how a complex system can collapse through its own co-evolution. The eighth exercise
builds one with credit links that are cut when a debtor's wealth falls below a threshold.

::: {#exr-complex-bank-toy}
#### A toy bank network

Ten banks on a ring each lend one unit to the next: $w_{i, i + 1} = 1$ means bank $i + 1$ owes bank $i$. Each step a
bank's wealth changes by a random shock (independent, normal with standard deviation $0.5$) plus $0.1$ per loan it has
made, and a lender cuts its loan when the debtor's wealth falls below zero. Starting from wealth 1 for all, simulate 50
steps with seed 2 and report the number of loans left. Is the system complex?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Yes: the weight $w_{i, i + 1}$ is set to zero according to the state of bank $i + 1$, and the wealth of bank $i$
depends on its loans. Each cut lowers the income of the lender, which makes it more likely to fall below zero in turn
and lose its own creditor; a chain of cuts can run around the ring. The number of loans left depends on the shocks.

## Python

The rule is simulated with NumPy, with the loans as a Boolean vector indexed by the lender.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
wealth, loans = np.ones(10), np.ones(10, dtype=bool)
history = []
for t in range(50):
    wealth += rng.normal(0, 0.5, 10) + 0.1 * loans
    loans &= ~(np.roll(wealth, -1) < 0)
    history.append(int(loans.sum()))
print("loans left at steps 10, 20, 30, 40, 50:", history[9::10])
```

```{.text .run-output}
loans left at steps 10, 20, 30, 40, 50: [7, 7, 5, 5, 5]
```
::::
:::

Hebb's rule stores a pattern in the weights, and the stored weights then make the pattern a fixed point of the state
dynamics. The ninth exercise proves this, which is the principle of associative memory.

::: {#exr-complex-hebb-memory}
#### A stored pattern is a fixed point

Let $\mathbf p \in \{-1, 1\}^N$ with $N \geq 2$, and let $w_{ij} = p_ip_j$ for $i \neq j$ and $w_{ii} = 0$ (the weights
Hebb's rule produces from zero after presenting $\mathbf p$, up to a factor). Prove that $\mathbf p$ is a fixed point of
$s_i \mapsto \operatorname{sign}(\sum_jw_{ij}s_j)$ and that so is $-\mathbf p$. Check that a pattern with 10 of 100
signs flipped returns to $\mathbf p$ in one step.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\sum_jw_{ij}p_j = \sum_{j \neq i}p_ip_j^2 = (N - 1)p_i$, whose sign is $p_i$ because $N \geq 2$. So $\mathbf p$ is
fixed, and by linearity in $\mathbf s$ so is $-\mathbf p$. If $\mathbf s$ differs from $\mathbf p$ in $k$ places, then
$\sum_jw_{ij}s_j = p_i\sum_{j \neq i}p_js_j$, and $\sum_{j \neq i}p_js_j \geq N - 1 - 2k$, which is positive when $k <
(N - 1)/2$: one step restores $\mathbf p$.

## Python

Check on $N = 100$ with 10 flipped signs.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
p = rng.choice([-1, 1], 100)
W = np.outer(p, p); np.fill_diagonal(W, 0)
s = p.copy(); s[rng.choice(100, 10, replace=False)] *= -1
print("errors before:", int((s != p).sum()), "after one step:", int((np.sign(W @ s) != p).sum()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
errors before: 10 after one step: 0
```
::::
:::

The last exercise combines co-evolution with the question of what a single element can know. It asks whether the
co-evolving voter model reaches the same state when rewiring is switched off.

::: {#exr-complex-voter-no-rewiring}
#### The voter model without co-evolution

Run `CoevolvingVoterSystem` with 200 voters and mean degree 4 for 100 steps, once with $q = 0$ (no rewiring: an
ordinary voter model on a fixed graph) and once with $q = 0.6$. Report the fraction of disagreeing links at the end and
the fraction of voters with opinion 1. Explain the difference.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $q = 0$ the graph is fixed and the system is not complex in the sense of @def-complex-system. Disagreement can
then only be removed by persuasion, so the ordinary voter model drifts towards one opinion: one opinion gains most
voters, while the links between the shrinking minority and the rest still disagree. With $q = 0.6$ most disagreeing
links are rewired instead of persuaded away, and the network fragments into groups of one opinion: disagreement nearly
vanishes, while both opinions keep a large share in separate groups. The two runs have the same elements and initial
states; only the weight rule differs.

## Python

The two runs use the same seed, so they start from the same graph and opinions.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.social.opinion_dynamics import CoevolvingVoterSystem
for q in (0.0, 0.6):
    run = simulate(CoevolvingVoterSystem(200, mean_degree=4, rewiring=q), until=100, random_state=0)
    op = run.get_values("voters.opinion")[-1]
    net = run.get_network(len(run.times) - 1)
    a, b = np.asarray(net.sources), np.asarray(net.targets)
    print(f"q = {q}: disagreeing links {(op[a] != op[b]).mean():.3f}, share of opinion 1 {op.mean():.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
q = 0.0: disagreeing links 0.059, share of opinion 1 0.945
q = 0.6: disagreeing links 0.005, share of opinion 1 0.715
```
::::
:::
::::

## Levels of description and emergence {#sec-levels-and-emergence}

Nobody describes the air in a room by the positions of its $10^{28}$ molecules, and nobody needs to: temperature,
pressure and density say what matters [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 1.2]. A description by a few
macroscopic variables is a coarse-graining, and the variables are a level of description. This section first defines
coarse-graining. It then proves why macroscopic variables of independent parts are sharp, which is the reason the
pressure of an ideal gas is not emergent [@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Sec. 1.1;
@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 8.1]. With that result in hand it defines emergent properties as
macroscopic properties that need the interactions, and order parameters as the macroscopic variables that detect a
broken symmetry [@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Secs. 2.2 and 2.5].

For more on this topic, see @jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023 [Chs. 1-3], @bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021 [Secs.
8.1.1, 8.1.4 and 8.1.5], @charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017 [Secs. 1.2 and 2.5], @satzMoreSumParts2022 [Ch. 1]
and @downeyThinkComplexity2018 [Ch. 9].

### Coarse-graining

A macroscopic description keeps some information about the microstate and forgets the rest. Mathematically it is a map
from microstates to a smaller set, and two microstates that the map sends to the same value are indistinguishable at
that level. The definition below names the map, its values and the level it defines; it does not require the coarse
level to have dynamics of its own, which is an extra property examined in the examples and exercises.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-coarse-graining}
#### Coarse-graining

Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of microstates of a system of interacting elements (@def-interacting-system). A
**coarse-graining** is a map $\pi : \mathcal S \to \mathcal Y$ onto a set $\mathcal Y$ of **macrostates**; the pair
$(\mathcal Y, \pi)$ is a **level of description**. The macrostate of $\mathbf s$ is $\pi(\mathbf s)$, and the
microstates with macrostate $y$ form the **fibre** $\pi^{-1}(y)$. A trajectory $\mathbf s(t)$ has the
**macro-trajectory** $y(t) = \pi(\mathbf s(t))$. A level $(\mathcal Y', \pi')$ is **coarser** than $(\mathcal Y, \pi)$
if $\pi' = \varphi \circ \pi$ for some map $\varphi : \mathcal Y \to \mathcal Y'$.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The most used coarse-graining of the tutorial is the magnetisation of a set of spins. Its fibres are counted by a
binomial coefficient, which is the first appearance of the counting behind entropy.

::: {#exm-coarse-magnetisation}
#### Magnetisation

For $N$ spins $s_i = \pm1$, $\pi(\mathbf s) = m = \frac1N\sum_is_i$ takes the $N + 1$ values $-1, -1 + \frac2N, \dots,
1$. The fibre of $m$ consists of the microstates with $N(1 + m)/2$ spins up, so $|\pi^{-1}(m)| = \binom{N}{N(1 +
m)/2}$. For $N = 100$ the fibre of $m = 0$ has about $10^{29}$ microstates and the fibre of $m = 1$ has one.
:::

A rigid body moves as one object, so its centre of mass is a complete description of its translation. Jensen uses this
to explain what a robust collective degree of freedom is.

::: {#exm-coarse-centre-of-mass}
#### Centre of mass

For $N$ particles of equal mass at positions $\mathbf x_i$, the centre of mass $\pi(\mathbf x_1, \dots, \mathbf x_N) =
\frac1N\sum_i\mathbf x_i$ is a coarse-graining to $\mathbb R^3$. For an iceberg, whose molecules move together, it
describes the motion completely (with the orientation); for a liquid it misses almost everything
[@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Sec. 2.2].
:::

Charbonneau defines the density of particles in a region by counting, the same procedure as a coarse-graining onto a
field. The figure shows that it gives a sharp value only on scales much larger than the distance between particles.

::: {#exm-coarse-density}
#### Density from counting

For $N$ points $\mathbf x_n$ in the unit square and a disc of radius $r$ about its centre, $\rho(r) = \frac{1}{\pi
r^2}\#\{n : \lVert\mathbf x_n - \mathbf c\rVert \leq r\}$ [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 1.2, eq.
(1.1)]. For radii comparable to the mean spacing $\delta \approx N^{-1/2}$ the value depends on where individual points
fall; for $r \gg \delta$ two independent placements give the same density $N$. A macroscopic variable exists because
the scales are separated.

![The density counted in discs of growing radius about the centre of the unit square, for two independent placements of
$10^6$ points. Below the mean spacing the two curves differ; above it both settle at $10^6$.](figures/micro_macro_density.svg){#fig-micro-macro-density width=70%}
:::

Block-spin coarse-graining replaces a block of spins by one spin, the majority of the block. Applied to independent
spins it acts on the probability of an up spin by an explicit map.

::: {#exm-coarse-block-majority}
#### Majority of three

Group the spins of a chain into blocks of three and replace each block by its majority. If the spins are independent
and up with probability $p$, a block is up when at least two of its spins are up, with probability
$$
R(p) = 3p^2(1 - p) + p^3 = 3p^2 - 2p^3 ,
$$
and different blocks are independent. The coarse level is again a chain of independent spins, with $p$ replaced by
$R(p)$. The map $R$ returns in the next section, as the mean-field law of majority rule.
:::

On a square lattice the blocks are $3 \times 3$, and the majority of nine spins decides the block spin. The figure
shows two Ising configurations from scikit-complexity and two rounds of this coarse-graining.

::: {#exm-coarse-ising-blocks}
#### Block majority of Ising configurations

Below the critical temperature, the Ising lattice consists of large domains, and block majority keeps them while
deleting the small islands, so the coarse lattices look ever more ordered. Above it, domains are small, and block
majority turns the configuration into ever more random-looking noise. The coarse-graining moves the two
configurations apart: a first glimpse of how a level of description can sharpen the difference between phases.

![Ising configurations on a $162 \times 162$ torus at $T = 1.8$ (top) and $T = 3.5$ (bottom), and their images under
one and two rounds of $3 \times 3$ block majority. The ordered configuration becomes more ordered and the disordered one
more disordered.](figures/block_majority.svg){#fig-block-majority width=95%}
:::

Two coarse-grainings of the same microstates can be compared when one factors through the other. Magnetisation and its
sign give the simplest example.

::: {#exm-coarse-coarser}
#### A coarser level

The sign of the magnetisation, $\pi'(\mathbf s) = \operatorname{sign}(m)$ with values in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$, is coarser than
$m$: $\pi' = \operatorname{sign} \circ \pi$. Each fibre of $\pi'$ is a union of fibres of $\pi$. The microstate is the
finest level of all ($\pi = $ identity), and the constant map to a single point is the coarsest.
:::

A coarse-graining need not commute with other operations on microstates. Block majority, unlike averaging, changes the
magnetisation.

::: {#exm-coarse-not-commuting}
#### Majority does not preserve the mean

For the chain $(+, +, -, +, -, -, +, +, -)$ the magnetisation is $1/9$. Its three blocks of three have majorities
$+, -, +$, with magnetisation $1/3$. Averaging blocks instead of taking their majority preserves the magnetisation:
$\frac13(\frac13 - \frac13 + \frac13) = \frac19$. So the block mean, but not the block majority, factors the
magnetisation through the coarse level.
:::

A macrostate can carry dynamics of its own, but need not. For a deterministic map $F$ on $\mathcal S$ the question is
whether $\pi(F(\mathbf s))$ is determined by $\pi(\mathbf s)$.

::: {#exm-coarse-closure}
#### Closed and open coarse levels

For the map $F(\mathbf s) = -\mathbf s$ that flips all spins, $m(F(\mathbf s)) = -m(\mathbf s)$: the macro level has
its own map $m \mapsto -m$, and we call it **closed**. For the Game of Life and $\pi$ the number of live cells, it is
not: a blinker of three cells has three live cells at the next step, while three isolated cells have none. The same
macrostate has different futures, so the number of live cells has no dynamics of its own.
:::

Markov chains on a finite set give a precise version of closure. Hoel, Albantakis and Tononi used a four-state chain
whose coarse-graining is closed and deterministic.

::: {#exm-coarse-lumping}
#### Lumping the states of a Markov chain

A chain on $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ moves from each of $0, 1, 2$ to one of $0, 1, 2$ uniformly at random, and from $3$ to $3$.
The partition $\{0, 1, 2\}, \{3\}$ is lumpable: every state of a block has the same probability of entering each block,
so the coarse process is a Markov chain, here the identity on two macrostates. scikit-complexity's `emergence` finds the
partition and the macro matrix.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import emergence
P = np.array([[1/3, 1/3, 1/3, 0], [1/3, 1/3, 1/3, 0], [1/3, 1/3, 1/3, 0], [0, 0, 0, 1]])
result = emergence(P, kind="causal")
print("partition:", result.partition, "macro matrix:", result.macro_matrix.tolist())
```

```{.text .run-output}
partition: [0 0 0 1] macro matrix: [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]
```
:::

A macroscopic variable can also average over time as well as over elements. The pressure of a gas is such a variable,
and its definition uses the whole trajectory over a time window.

::: {#exm-coarse-time-average}
#### Pressure as a time average

The pressure on a wall of area $A$ is the momentum transferred to it per unit time and area. Over a window $[t, t +
\tau]$ it is $p = \frac{1}{A\tau}\sum 2m v_\perp$, summed over the collisions with the wall in the window. This is a
coarse-graining of the trajectory on $[t, t + \tau]$ rather than of one microstate, and it is sharp when the window
contains many collisions [@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023, Sec. 1.1].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the fibre sizes of the magnetisation. They add up to the number of microstates, since the
fibres partition $\mathcal S$.

::: {#exr-coarse-fibres}
#### Fibres of the magnetisation

For $N = 10$ spins, list $|\pi^{-1}(m)|$ for every value of $m$, check that they add up to $2^{10}$, and find the
fraction of microstates with $|m| \leq 0.2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The value $m = (2k - 10)/10$ corresponds to $k$ spins up, so the fibre has $\binom{10}{k}$ elements, $k = 0, \dots,
10$. They add up to $(1 + 1)^{10} = 1024$ by the binomial theorem. The values $|m| \leq 0.2$ are $k = 4, 5, 6$, with
$210 + 252 + 210 = 672$ microstates, a fraction $672/1024 \approx 0.656$.

## Python

The binomial coefficients are listed with `math.comb`.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
N = 10
sizes = {(2 * k - N) / N: comb(N, k) for k in range(N + 1)}
print(sizes)
print("total:", sum(sizes.values()), "| fraction with |m| <= 0.2:", sum(v for m, v in sizes.items() if abs(m) <= 0.2 + 1e-12) / 2**N)
```

```{.text .run-output}
{-1.0: 1, -0.8: 10, -0.6: 45, -0.4: 120, -0.2: 210, 0.0: 252, 0.2: 210, 0.4: 120, 0.6: 45, 0.8: 10, 1.0: 1}
total: 1024 | fraction with |m| <= 0.2: 0.65625
```
::::
:::

The map $R$ of @exm-coarse-block-majority follows from counting. The second exercise derives it and checks it against
a sample of random blocks.

::: {#exr-coarse-majority-map}
#### The block-majority map

Prove that the majority of three independent spins, each up with probability $p$, is up with probability $R(p) = 3p^2
- 2p^3$, and that $R(1 - p) = 1 - R(p)$. Check $R(0.6)$ on $10^6$ random blocks.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The number of up spins in a block is binomial with parameters $3$ and $p$. The majority is up when it is $2$ or $3$,
with probability $\binom32p^2(1 - p) + p^3 = 3p^2 - 2p^3$. A block's majority is down exactly when the majority of the
reversed block is up, and reversing turns probability $p$ into $1 - p$, so $1 - R(p) = R(1 - p)$. Directly: $R(1 - p) =
3(1 - p)^2 - 2(1 - p)^3 = 1 - 3p^2 + 2p^3$.

## Python

Check on $10^6$ blocks of three spins with $p = 0.6$, where $R(0.6) = 0.648$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
p = 0.6
blocks = rng.random((10**6, 3)) < p
print(f"R(0.6) = {3 * p**2 - 2 * p**3:.4f}; sampled: {(blocks.sum(1) >= 2).mean():.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
R(0.6) = 0.6480; sampled: 0.6482
```
::::
:::

Coarser levels are composed from finer ones. The third exercise proves that "coarser than" is transitive and checks a
chain of three levels on a small system.

::: {#exr-coarse-transitive}
#### Coarser is transitive

Prove that if $\pi'$ is coarser than $\pi$ and $\pi''$ is coarser than $\pi'$, then $\pi''$ is coarser than $\pi$, and
that every fibre of a coarser level is a union of fibres of the finer one. Check the second statement for $N = 4$ spins
with $\pi = $ the microstate, $\pi' = m$ and $\pi'' = |m|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $\pi' = \varphi \circ \pi$ and $\pi'' = \psi \circ \pi'$, then $\pi'' = (\psi \circ \varphi) \circ \pi$. For a
macrostate $y'$ of $\pi'$, $\pi'^{-1}(y') = \{\mathbf s : \varphi(\pi(\mathbf s)) = y'\} = \bigcup_{y \in
\varphi^{-1}(y')}\pi^{-1}(y)$, a union of fibres of $\pi$.

## Python

Check on the 16 microstates of four spins: each fibre of $|m|$ is the union of the fibres of $m$ with that absolute
value.

```{.python .run}
from itertools import product
states = list(product([-1, 1], repeat=4))
m = {s: sum(s) / 4 for s in states}
fibre_m = {}
for s in states:
    fibre_m.setdefault(m[s], set()).add(s)
for a in sorted({abs(v) for v in m.values()}):
    fibre_abs = {s for s in states if abs(m[s]) == a}
    union = set().union(*(f for v, f in fibre_m.items() if abs(v) == a))
    print(f"|m| = {a}: {len(fibre_abs)} microstates, union of m-fibres: {fibre_abs == union}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
|m| = 0.0: 6 microstates, union of m-fibres: True
|m| = 0.5: 8 microstates, union of m-fibres: True
|m| = 1.0: 2 microstates, union of m-fibres: True
```
::::
:::

Whether a coarse level has dynamics of its own can be tested on two microstates with the same macrostate. The fourth
exercise does this for the Game of Life with scikit-complexity.

::: {#exr-coarse-life-not-closed}
#### The number of live cells is not closed

Start `GameOfLifeSystem` on an $8 \times 8$ torus from a blinker (three cells in a row) and from three isolated cells.
Show that both have three live cells and compute the number at the next step. Conclude that the number of live cells is
not a closed coarse level.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The blinker has three live cells at every step (@exr-interacting-blinker). Three isolated cells each have no live
neighbour and die, and no dead cell has three live neighbours, so the next state is empty. Two microstates with the
same macrostate $3$ have macrostates $3$ and $0$ one step later, so there is no map $\bar F$ with $\pi \circ F = \bar F
\circ \pi$.

## Python

The two initial configurations are passed with `initial`.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.computer_science.automata import GameOfLifeSystem
blinker = np.zeros((8, 8)); blinker[3, 2:5] = 1
isolated = np.zeros((8, 8)); isolated[1, 1] = isolated[4, 4] = isolated[6, 1] = 1
for name, start in [("blinker", blinker), ("isolated", isolated)]:
    frames = simulate(GameOfLifeSystem((8, 8), initial=start), until=1).get_lattice("cells.alive")
    print(f"{name}: live cells {int(frames[0].sum())} -> {int(frames[1].sum())}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
blinker: live cells 3 -> 3
isolated: live cells 3 -> 0
```
::::
:::

Charbonneau's density counts points in discs. The fifth exercise computes the relative spread of the count, which
explains where the macroscopic regime of @fig-micro-macro-density begins.

::: {#exr-coarse-density-spread}
#### When is a density sharp?

For $N$ independent uniform points in the unit square and a disc of radius $r$ inside it, the count is binomial with
parameters $N$ and $\pi r^2$. Show that its relative standard deviation is $\sqrt{(1 - \pi r^2)/(N\pi r^2)}$, evaluate
it for $N = 10^6$ at $r = 10^{-3}$, $10^{-2}$ and $10^{-1}$, and compare with 400 sampled placements at $r = 10^{-2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each point falls in the disc independently with probability $q = \pi r^2$, so the count has mean $Nq$ and variance
$Nq(1 - q)$, and relative standard deviation $\sqrt{(1 - q)/(Nq)}$. For $N = 10^6$ this is about $0.56$ at $r =
10^{-3}$ (a disc holding about three points), $0.056$ at $r = 10^{-2}$ and $0.0055$ at $r = 10^{-1}$. The density is
sharp once the disc holds many points, that is $r \gg N^{-1/2} = 10^{-3}$.

## Python

The formula is evaluated, and the count is sampled directly as a binomial variable, which is its exact law.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
N = 10**6
for r in (1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1):
    q = np.pi * r**2
    print(f"r = {r:g}: relative sd {np.sqrt((1 - q) / (N * q)):.4f}")
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
counts = rng.binomial(N, np.pi * 1e-4, size=400)
print(f"sampled at r = 0.01: {counts.std() / counts.mean():.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
r = 0.001: relative sd 0.5642
r = 0.01: relative sd 0.0564
r = 0.1: relative sd 0.0056
sampled at r = 0.01: 0.0545
```
::::
:::

Block majority of a lattice can be iterated, and the fraction of up spins at each level shows where the
coarse-graining leads. The sixth exercise does this for configurations of `IsingSystem`.

::: {#exr-coarse-ising-flow}
#### Iterated block majority of Ising configurations

Equilibrate `IsingSystem` on a $162 \times 162$ torus at $T = 1.8$ (started from all spins up) and at $T = 3.5$, and
